title: J.P. Morgan global market strategist on tech stock selloff
summary: After one of the worst routs for US tech stocks in years, shares steadied as investors weighed whether the AI investment boom will slow now that Democrats have won broadly in the midterms. NBC News' Christine Romans asks Jordan Jackson, global market strategist at J.P. Morgan, how much the election and data-centre politics change the outlook for AI spending. Jackson argues the long-term case for AI investment is intact and that the selloff could be a buying opportunity for patient investors.
focus: Shadow Romans' opening set-up of the week's market moves and Jackson's answer on why the selloff may be an opportunity; both are short, clearly paced stretches of market vocabulary (no transcript was available this run, so vocabulary is drawn from same-day coverage of the selloff).

vocab.meaning: one of the giant cloud companies that build and run huge data centres
vocab.context: The giant cloud providers are the ones whose AI spending plans investors are now questioning after the rout.
vocab.example: Three hyperscalers account for most of the demand in this market, so customer concentration is our biggest risk.

vocab.meaning: the single point that limits how fast a whole process can move
vocab.context: Analysts covering the selloff argue that electricity, not chips, is what really limits how fast AI data centres can be built.
vocab.example: Approval from the regional office is the real bottleneck, so let's fix that before we hire more staff.

vocab.meaning: heavy, widespread damage or losses (used loosely for a market crash)
vocab.zh: 惨重损失；大屠杀（喻股市暴跌）
vocab.context: Business anchors used the word to describe how badly tech shares were hit on the worst day of the week.
vocab.example: After the carnage in last quarter's results, the board wants a credible turnaround plan, not more slides.

vocab.context: Coverage of the rout described tech and chip stocks as having been wiped out in a single session.
vocab.example: A low-cost entrant could obliterate our margins in this segment within two years.

vocab.meaning: to be unsteady, close to falling one way or the other
vocab.context: Tech shares were described as wobbling on the edge of a deeper decline before buyers returned.
vocab.example: The deal is teetering on the edge, so the partners need to call the CFO today.

vocab.context: The week's coverage pointed to earlier failed bets in the AI space as a warning about overspending.
vocab.example: The ERP rollout was a debacle, and we're still cleaning up the data two years later.

vocab.meaning: a small, short-lived change that doesn't affect the overall trend
vocab.context: Strategists debated whether the crash was a temporary blip or the start of a longer reassessment of AI.
vocab.example: The dip in Q3 churn looks like a blip, but let's watch two more months before we celebrate.

vocab.meaning: to lose something, especially money, quickly and in large amounts
vocab.context: Investors worry about AI projects that keep losing cash at a fast rate before they earn anything back.
vocab.example: The startup is haemorrhaging cash on customer acquisition, so its runway is shorter than the deck suggests.

vocab.meaning: an obstacle or difficulty that must be overcome
vocab.context: New local opposition and tougher approvals were described as fresh obstacles for data-centre builders.
vocab.example: Regulatory approval is the last hurdle before we can close the acquisition.

vocab.meaning: how investors have arranged their holdings and bets in the market
vocab.context: Part of the selloff was blamed on how heavily investors had piled into the same chip stocks beforehand.
vocab.example: Before the pitch, map competitors' positioning so we can show the client where the white space is.

vocab.meaning: to reverse or close out a position or arrangement
vocab.context: Analysts said heavily borrowed bets on AI stocks were being reversed all at once, which deepened the fall.
vocab.example: Unwinding the joint venture will take longer than setting it up, so plan for a 12-month exit.

vocab.meaning: to sell something quickly and in large amounts, often at a loss
vocab.context: Investors sold chip and AI shares in large volumes on the day after the election results.
vocab.example: If the lock-up expires in March, early investors may dump their shares and pressure the price.

vocab.context: The Nasdaq fell sharply on Thursday before tech shares steadied on Friday.
vocab.example: Our win rate tumbled after the price increase, which suggests we overestimated willingness to pay.

vocab.meaning: having fallen so far, so fast, that the price may now be too low
vocab.context: After the steep drop, some analysts argued AI and chip stocks had been pushed below what their fundamentals justify.
vocab.example: The sector looks oversold, so this may be a good moment to approach targets about an acquisition.

phrases.meaning: a fall of 10% or more from a recent peak
phrases.zh: 进入调整区间（较高点下跌10%以上）
phrases.context: The Nasdaq closed the worst day of the week down more than 10% from its high.
phrases.example: Once the stock slips into correction territory, the activist investor will have a stronger case for change.

phrases.meaning: an investment that so many people already hold that it can fall hard when they all sell
phrases.zh: 拥挤交易（大量投资者持有同一头寸）
phrases.context: Semiconductors were described as the market's most crowded bet before the selloff began.
phrases.example: Data-centre real estate has become a crowded trade, so our client should look at adjacent niches instead.

phrases.meaning: a situation in which buyers refuse to buy, pushing prices down
phrases.zh: 买方罢工（买家集体观望不买）
phrases.context: Market commentators used the term to describe investors refusing to step in and buy tech shares.
phrases.example: Procurement teams are on a buyer's strike until the new budget is approved, so expect a slow Q4 pipeline.

phrases.meaning: very quickly and in large amounts (usually money)
phrases.zh: 大量而迅速地（赚钱或赔钱）
phrases.context: Retail investors were described as selling tech stocks rapidly and in large amounts during the rout.
phrases.example: The incumbent was losing customers hand over fist until it fixed its onboarding process.

phrases.meaning: to start getting involved in something gradually or cautiously
phrases.context: Strategists suggested investors could step back into tech slowly rather than all at once.
phrases.example: Let's wade into the Southeast Asian market with one pilot country before committing a full team.
